result.summary: Pausanias searches the old epics for the sons of Polycaon and Messene and finds nothing. He then traces the Messenian kings from Perieres to Aphareus, discusses rival claims about the location of Œchalia, and records the arrival of Neleus and Lycus and the family of Aphareus.

scenes.title: Searching the poets for Polycaon
scenes.summary: Pausanias consults the epic poems and genealogists but finds no mention of Messene's husband or sons. The poems list Polycaon's line and then introduce King Perieres.

scenes.title: Melaneus and the disputed Œchalia
scenes.summary: Messenians say Melaneus came to Perieres and received Carnasium, once called Œchalia. Thessalians, Eubœans and Hecatæus place Œchalia elsewhere, but Pausanias favors the Messenian account.

scenes.title: Aphareus and his guests
scenes.summary: Aphareus rules Messenia, builds Arene, and receives Neleus, who settles at Pylos. Lycus arrives from Athens and teaches the mysteries of the Great Goddesses.
scenes.stakes: Neleus and Lycus are exiles fleeing powerful kinsmen, Pelias and Ægeus.

scenes.title: Idas, Lynceus and their descendants
scenes.summary: Idas and Lynceus are described, with Lynceus's keen sight. Idas's daughter Cleopatra and the wives Marpessa and Polydora are linked, and all three are said to have died by suicide.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias skeptically reports Pindar's claim that Lynceus could see through a tree trunk.
Pausanias remarks that Greek events are almost always the subject of disputed accounts.

analysis.text: Pausanias weighs conflicting traditions and epic sources, favoring local Messenian accounts when they seem most probable.
The chapter shows how Greek genealogies were assembled from lost epics such as the Eœæ and linked heroic families across regions.

fun_facts.text: The Great Eœæ, Cyprian Poems and works of Cinæthon and Asius cited here survive only in fragments, so Pausanias preserves information about them.

language_notes.text: The Great Eœæ (Catalogue of Women) and the Naupactian Poems were early Greek epics on heroines and genealogies; Cinæthon and Asius were early genealogical poets.
Melaneus was thought Apollo's son because of his archery; Apollo was the archer god. Œchalia was supposedly named for his wife.
Uterine sister means a sister by the same mother, not the same father.
Neleus is called the son of Cretheus, but Poseidon is given as his surname-father: Pausanias reports the tradition that Æolus was surnamed Poseidon.
The Great Goddesses are Demeter and Persephone, whose mysteries were secret rites open only to initiates.
"Believe it who will" signals Pausanias' open scepticism toward Pindar's marvellous claim.
Protesilaus was reputed the first Greek to die at Troy, leaping ashore first; the Cyprian Poems told of events before the Iliad.

context_notes.text: Hecatæus of Miletus was an early historian and geographer, active around 500 BC. Eretria was a city on Eubœa.
Lycus, son of Pandion, was exiled from Athens in a dispute with his brother Ægeus, according to Athenian tradition.
Meleager was the Calydonian hero known for the boar hunt; Cleopatra was his wife.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias' aside shows his habit of weighing rival traditions as a critical, slightly weary researcher.
Lynceus' ability to see through a tree trunk exaggerates keen sight to legendary extremes.
